show_hn_title: Show HN: BackDown – local drive inventory and hash-based duplicate checks
first_comment:
I’m working on BackDown, a local drive-inventory and duplicate-checking tool.

BackDown began as a one-off job to consolidate years of old drives into one archive. The original scripts indexed about 27 million files and read and hashed 15 TB in that founding dataset. Those numbers describe that particular archive, not a general performance claim.

The current public build is v0.2.0-alpha.4. It provides index, hash, dupes and check commands, plus a local browser and read-only viewers for supported files. Builds cover Linux x86-64 and ARM64, macOS universal, and Windows x86-64.

Download and setup notes: https://backdown.io/download/

There is no signup gate. The local edition needs no account and sends no telemetry. This is an early alpha, rather than the planned polished native desktop release. Broader planning and copying workflows are still roadmap work.

Useful feedback would include confusing inventory results, content comparisons that need more explanation, and reproducible browser or viewer problems. Please use non-sensitive examples; sharing a private archive is not necessary.

response_templates.question: What can I use today?
response_templates.reply: The public v0.2.0-alpha.4 includes index, hash, dupes and check commands, a local browser and read-only viewers for supported files. It is a command-line alpha for Linux, macOS and Windows. Download and setup notes: https://backdown.io/download/

response_templates.question: Does this replace my backup?
response_templates.reply: BackDown helps you inventory drives and inspect matching file contents. Duplicate results need to be interpreted within your backup plan: a second copy may be one you should keep. The public alpha is useful for examining the copies you have.

response_templates.question: Will it automatically delete my files?
response_templates.reply: The alpha inspection workflow uses index, hash, dupes and check to examine your data and report results. A duplicate finding is not an instruction to delete. Broader planning, copying and cleanup workflows are planned work; we are not presenting them as shipped alpha features.

response_templates.question: Can I rely on a matching hash to clear a drive?
response_templates.reply: A matching content hash is evidence about the files compared. Review the full scan and check results, including anything unscanned or unique, and confirm which copies your backup plan needs before making a deletion decision. BackDown is still an alpha.

response_templates.question: Do my files get uploaded?
response_templates.reply: The local edition works on your machine, needs no account and sends no telemetry. Its file browser is served locally. Early access is an optional signup for one email when BackDown is ready, separate from downloading or using the alpha.

response_templates.question: Which operating systems are supported?
response_templates.reply: The current alpha has Linux x86-64 and ARM64 builds, a macOS universal build for Apple silicon and Intel, and a Windows x86-64 build. Release checksums and setup notes are at https://backdown.io/download/

response_templates.question: Is there a finished desktop app?
response_templates.reply: There is a local browser interface in the public command-line alpha. A polished native desktop experience is planned. Current release details and roadmap status are available at https://backdown.io/status/

response_templates.question: Is it AI?
response_templates.reply: The capabilities discussed here are drive indexing, content hashing, duplicate checks and local file viewing. We are not claiming that the public alpha uses AI to understand your archive.

response_templates.question: Will I save 5.9 TB?
response_templates.reply: The 5.9 TB figure comes from duplication found on the largest drive in BackDown’s founding archive. It is one real dataset, not a saving to expect on another archive. Your results depend on the contents of your drives.

response_templates.question: Do I need to join the list to download?
response_templates.reply: No. The alpha is available directly at https://backdown.io/download/ with no email signup gate. Join early access for one email when BackDown is ready; signing up is optional.

response_templates.question: How should I report a problem?
response_templates.reply: Tell us the version, operating system, what you expected and what happened. A small example using non-sensitive files is ideal. Remove private filenames, paths and contents from any logs or screenshots you choose to share.

response_templates.question: Is source mounting automatically read-only?
response_templates.reply: The founding archive job used source drives mounted read-only. That describes how that job was run; it is not a claim that the public alpha automatically changes every drive’s mount permissions.

posts.title: An identical copy still has a job
posts.visual_headline: An identical copy can be worth keeping.
posts.visual_subhead: Matching content tells you what is duplicated. Your backup plan determines which copies you still need.
posts.linkedin_copy:
Two files can contain the same bytes and still serve different purposes.

A second copy on another drive may be part of your backup plan. A repeated folder on the same drive may simply be taking up room. Seeing “duplicate” is the beginning of a decision, not an instruction to delete.

BackDown's alpha helps identify matching content across indexed drives. That gives you a clearer inventory of the copies you have.

Before removing anything, consider which drive holds each copy, whether the data matters, and how you would recover it if a drive failed. A duplicate report cannot make those choices for you.

posts.title: Put evidence behind the comparison
posts.visual_headline: Compare the contents. Keep the evidence.
posts.visual_subhead: SHA-256 checks help establish whether files match. A filename alone cannot answer that question.
posts.linkedin_copy:
A folder name is a label. A content hash gives you evidence about the file itself.

BackDown uses SHA-256 hashing when checking matching file contents. The public alpha includes index, hash, dupes and check commands, so you can move from a list of files to a more informed view of where the matching copies are.

That distinction matters when an archive contains renamed files, repeated exports and years of copied folders. Familiar names can hide different contents; different names can point to matching data.

The result still needs to be read in the context of the drives and files you have scanned. It is evidence to inspect when planning your archive.

posts.title: Names do not prove content
posts.visual_headline: Same name does not prove same file.
posts.visual_subhead: Renaming a file changes its label. Hashing compares its contents, helping you inspect the copies behind the names.
posts.linkedin_copy:
Consider two files both named “holiday.jpg”. They could be different photos.

Now consider “holiday.jpg” and “holiday-copy.jpg”. They could contain exactly the same photo data.

Names help people organise things, but they do not establish that file contents match. That becomes a problem when years of exports, renamed folders and device backups meet in one archive.

BackDown's alpha uses content hashing as part of its duplicate checks. It helps you investigate copies by their data, while keeping the paths available so you can understand where the results came from.

A match is still something to interpret within your backup plan. Start with evidence, then decide which copies serve a purpose.
